newsitem.title: USA: Soybean parasite not big threat to Ohio yields.
newsitem.headline: Soybean parasite not big threat to Ohio yields.

text.p: Soybean cyst nematodes do not pose a significant threat to this year's Ohio soybean crop despite the parasite's high profile, crop experts said.

"We've seen a few fields of continuous (non-rotated) soybeans that are at high levels, but it's not a yield-limiting factor for most farmers," said Paul Lipps, extension plant pathologist at the Ohio Agricultural Research and Development Center in Wooster, Ohio.
Soybean cyst nematodes decrease a soybean plant's root surface area and usually have an ill affect on the plant's yields, agronomists said.
A recent study by researchers at Ohio State University indicated that soybean cyst nematode infestation has been on the rise since the pest was first detected in Ohio in 1988.
"It's a growing problem in Ohio and throughout the Midwest," said Paulette Pierson, a plant pathologist and author of the study at Ohio State University.
But despite the increased incidence of the soybean cyst nematode in Ohio, there were no factors during this year's growing season that boosted the spread of the pest, agronomists said.
"Drought can intensify the presence of the cyst nematode, but we certainly didn't see any of that this year," Lipps said.
Cash grain sources throughout Ohio reported that there had been little talk among producers during this growing season about outbreaks of the soybean cyst nematode.
"It varies from field to field, but it is not a major problem around here," one Ohio-based grain merchandiser said.
Soybean cyst nematodes can be controlled through crop rotation and there are also nematode-resist varieties of soybeans available, industry sources said.
